Latest Update: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to massive issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to massive issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he indicates he has identified the next massive shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he notes can yield “small data” solutions to significant issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having remarked that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a fresh paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Sources indicate that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

In a recent development, having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of owners, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Recent findings suggest that ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Industry observers note that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Sources indicate that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing latest here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

According to recent reports, ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one organization or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

According to recent reports, you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Fresh tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

According to recent reports, ng: In AI, data cleaning is vital, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention swiftly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

In a recent development, for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an vital tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Industry observers note that ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

According to recent reports, “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion owners. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

It has been revealed that to make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

According to recent reports, one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

In a recent development, how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift glitch. I find it really vital to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and patch the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent latest neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s crucial for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

In a recent development, ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

10 'Find Hub' Hacks Every Android User Should Know

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone.
  • This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually.
  • There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone. Over the past year, Google has consistently added features to manage your belongings, share your location with loved ones, and locate lost devices. Find Hub can now notify you when you've left your device or your tracker behind. Plus, you can use Gemini to remember where you left items, even without a tracker attached. Behind the scenes, there are even more hidden settings and features to help track your devices and make it easier to retrieve them in case they are stolen or misplaced. If you use Find Hub, you need to know about these 10 hacks.

This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually. AirTags consumers should be familiar with this feature already. When you leave your tracker or device behind, and exit the location range, you’ll receive a notification that you left without your item. You need to enable this feature on a per-device basis. Go to Find Hub and select a device. Tap the settings gear icon next to the device's name, and enable Notify when left behind. While you’re here, go to Add location to add familiar locations where you don’t want to get a notification (like your home or workspace). Otherwise, Find Hub may spam you with left behind alerts.

There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker. You can simply ask Gemini to remember where you put things, and it will show up in the Find Hub app. To use it, pull up Gemini and say something like, “Remember in Find Hub that the passport is in the downstairs wardrobe,” or “I’ve kept the spare car keys behind the garage door.”.

Recent findings suggest that you can then ask Gemini, “Where did I keep my passport?” and it will tell you. If you change the location of an item, just ask Gemini to patch it for you. When you go to the Remembered tab, you’ll see the location of all remembered items. You can also add items manually here using the Add button.

Some Android smartphones can remain findable for several hours after they've been switched off or their batteries have run out. If you’re using a supported device (like the latest Pixel series smartphone), you can use a hardware feature to track the location using Google’s mesh network, relying on nearby devices (similar to how Android tags work).

Sources indicate that to make sure this feature is enabled, go to Find Hub, and tap Find your offline devices. Here, make sure that either With network in busy places only or With network everywhere is selected.

It has been revealed that if you’re using a tracker in your car, luggage, or on your keys, you might want to share location access with your spouse or family members. Find Hub has a feature called "Share Ownership" that lets you share the tracker details with up to 10 people. Only the location of your tracker is shared, not your personal device.

To set it up, go to Find Hub, and choose the tracker or accessory that you want to share. Tap the Share Ownership button and follow the on-screen instructions to share the invite link via a messaging app or using Quick Share. Once the recipient taps Accept, you’ll get a notification. Go to the device settings in Find Hub and tap the Confirm button to enable location sharing.

According to recent reports, you can swiftly share your live location with your friends or loved ones using Google Messages. Open a conversation, tap the Attachment icon, and choose Real-time location. Set the duration and tap Send.

It has been revealed that if you don’t like using the Messages app, you can do so directly from Find Hub. Go to the People tab at the bottom of the screen, and tap the Plus icon. Choose the duration and select a contact to share the location with, then tap the Get Link button to copy the link. You can then share it via any messaging app of your choice.

You might have a Find Hub tracker in your luggage to help keep tabs on your bags. But you don't have to be the only one privy to its location. If your airline loses that luggage, you can temporarily share its location with your airline to help you retrieve it. This is an official feature, too: Google partnered with multiple airlines to make this data sharing easier. From the Find Hub, choose your tracker. Tap the Share Item Location button, and then tap Share Item Location again. Copy the generated web link and share it with your airline using the app or support page. The link will automatically expire in seven days, so you don't have to worry about your airline continuing to monitor your luggage's location long after your flight.

Find Hub uses a mesh network of supported Android devices to securely locate your lost device or tag. But by default, it waits until multiple Android devices detect the location of the lost device. This works well if you've lost the device in crowded areas, but it can increase your wait time if you lose it somewhere remote. Luckily, there is a hidden setting that triggers location sharing even if a single device reports its location. Go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub > Find your offline devices and select With network everywhere instead of With network in busy places only.

If you’ve lost your smartphone, you don’t need to rush to a computer or a website to track it. Borrow someone’s Android smartphone and head into their Find Hub. Tap Sign in as guest and sign in with your Google account associated with your device, then find and select your device in the account. If requested, enter the PIN that you’ve previously set up. You can now track the device’s location, get directions to the device, or play a sound to help track the device if it’s nearby. If the device is truly lost, you can use the Mark as Lost feature to remotely lock your device.

Industry observers note that map-based tracking is helpful in getting to the general vicinity of your lost device. But your smartphone or tracker is hidden; finding it may require precision tracking. Many newer trackers like the Pixel Tag come with an ultra-wideband chip that helps you find the exact location of the tracker, given you are nearby. This also works on Pixel smartphones (Pixel 8 Pro series and above) and Samsung Galaxy devices (S21 and above, Plus and Ultra models only).

When using this feature, make sure you have Bluetooth enabled on your smartphone, then open Find Hub. Choose your tracker, and tap Find Nearby. Follow the on-screen instructions to locate the nearby device. You can also tap Play Sound to make the location process easier.

If you think your Android smartphone is lost or stolen, don’t rush to erase all data. While a remote factory reset is great for protecting your data, it also removes the device from your account. It’s best to try to get the device back. Two-factor authentication (or a passkey) on your Google account, along with a biometric lock on your smartphone, will protect the data itself.

Go to the Find Hub website, or use Find Hub on someone else’s phone in guest mode. Choose your device, and instead of Factory Reset, choose Mark as Lost. Here, you’ll see an option to enter a message. Type an alternative contact number, and a message to help recover the device.

UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.
  • Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue ….
  • In a recent development, the story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue ….

In a recent development, the story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022. This extended end-to-end encryption to almost all your iCloud data, meaning Apple has no access, and therefore cannot grant access to any government agencies who come knocking on its door.

The feature is off by default because it means Apple cannot help you access any of your data if, for example, you forget your iCloud password. However, those who want to maximize the privacy of their iCloud account can enable it.

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

This would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve mentioned many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

It would have been illegal for Apple to reveal that it had been instructed to compromise the privacy of customer data, but the firm found a clever way to effectively communicate this without breaking the law. Apple unveiled it was withdrawing ADP from the UK without explaining its reason.

It has been revealed that “Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”.

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP ….

Sources indicate that at this point, it was an open secret. However, ridiculously, despite the fact that everyone in the security and privacy field knew about it and was talking about it, Apple was still not allowed to officially confirm it.

The iPhone maker asked the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) to allow it to openly discuss the order, with privacy campaigners backing this call. The Financial Times reports that the court has now ruled in Apple’s favor.

It has been revealed that the UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal stated. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it rolled out – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

In a recent development, this ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

  • Sources indicate that the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027.
  • Sources indicate that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what owners need to know.

Sources indicate that the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

Sources indicate that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly claims it has no aims for a native Mac app.

Recent findings suggest that you can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft intends to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the tech giant.

Sources indicate that the June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

In a recent development, does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:.

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team prepares. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, type-C is C11 with the types C is missing: variants that match checks, distinct types for ids and units, generic types, and errors as values with try and defer. Its compiler, typec, takes the command line of cc, turns Type-C into C that you can read, and hands that C to your C compiler. A C11 file is already a Type-C file, so a program adopts it one file at a time.

Type-C is early: every example on this page works today, and the rest of the language is designed but not built yet (Status).

With Homebrew, on macOS or Linux:.

Homebrew builds typec from the release source with OCaml and dune. typec hands its C to cc unless told otherwise (Choosing the backend). To build it from a checkout instead, see Try it.

Recent findings suggest that an evaluator of arithmetic expression trees, which reports a division by zero or an overflow as a value instead of crashing. Like every C and Type-C example in this README, it is checked by the tests.

It builds with the options of cc and prints:.

What Type-C adds to C explains each fresh piece, and reveals the mistakes each one rules out. The tutorial grows a C program into Type-C one feature at a time, and the language reference states the rules of each construct.

According to recent reports, each feature below rules out a kind of mistake that C compiles without a word: as an error that the section demonstrates, or by making the mistake impossible to write. Where a C warning catches a form of it, the section claims which. The messages are those that typec prints, with its exit status in brackets (What typec reports). The cases of a variant are its constructors, as the messages call them.

A tagged union in C, with two bugs:.

The same in Type-C. Each field belongs to its case, so the wrong-member read cannot be written, and the forgotten case stops the build:.

C's -Wall warns of a forgotten enumerator only in a switch with no default, and only when the kind has an enumeration type; a default written for a kind that is none of the three, or an int kind, hides it (-Wswitch-enum warns with the default too). No flag that test/run/comparison.t tries warns of the wrong-member read. A match needs no default: it stops the program on a value whose tag is none of the cases, and a case added later is an error at every match that misses it.

According to recent reports, if (case ...) tests for one case and binds its fields, and while (case ...) loops while it holds. Outside them and match, Type-C code cannot name a field at all:.

A field read as C reads a member of the union:.

An arm of a match that can run into the next one is an error: it ends in break, return, continue, goto or a call that does not return.

In C, GCC's -Wextra warns of a missing break, and Clang does with -Wimplicit-fallthrough.

Sources indicate that A distinct type has the representation of another type but does not convert to it, or from it, without a cast. Ids and units that C would mix become an error:.

With C's typedef, the swap compiles, and no warning flag that comparison.t tries catches it:.

Recent findings suggest that an interface file, .tci, is a header for Type-C: other files include it with #include. A private type in it can be made only in the interface and in the source file of the same name, here port.tc; other files use ports and read their value. So, short of C code or reinterpreted storage (limits), every port but the zero value, {0}, comes from port_parse.

A type can take type parameters, instead of holding a void *. list(int) and list(double) are different types, so a list of prices cannot reach a function that sums integers. Each list(int) names the same type, wherever it is written.

Each instance of a generic type is a C structure of its own, and a structure converts to no other type, so typec refuses list(double) where list(int) is wanted:.

The C list of void * takes any element:.

It has been revealed that option(T) is a generic variant that every Type-C file has: None, or Some of a value. It replaces the -1 or NULL that means "not found", which a caller can forget to test:.

result(T, E) is another generic variant that every Type-C file has: Ok of a value, or Err of an error, which can be a variant with fields of its own. try gives the value of a result, or returns its error from the function at once:.

A call that drops a result, as a statement of its own, is an error:.

C drops a return code without a word unless its function is declared [[nodiscard]] (C23) or warn_unused_result, and then it warns.

C releases resources at one label that each error path must jump to; here an error path written later returns past it:.

A defer, written on the line after an acquisition, releases the resource at every exit after it: each exit runs the deferred statements in force there, in reverse order, so the return in the loop closes both files. A deferred statement cannot report an error, so the function flushes out itself before its last exit:.

Sources indicate that typec writes a copy of each deferred statement at each exit (What the C looks like). An analyzer finds some leaks of C by following paths: GCC's -fanalyzer reports both of copy.c, in either order.

A match with a default covers a upcoming case as C's default does; but a default that covers no case is refused, so one cannot be written "just in case" before the case exists. A value whose tag is none of its cases, which C code, casts and unions can make, stops the program when it is matched, at run time. private binds Type-C files only: C code reads and writes the layout as C does, the zero value is open to every file, and Type-C code that reinterprets storage, as *(port *)p does, is not refused. The guarantees and what each depends on are in design 14.

Type-C enters a program one file at a time. Take a small C program: main.c calls calc.c through calc.h.

calc.c becomes calc.tc, which parses a line into a variant and matches on it. It still includes calc.h, and calc_apply keeps its C type, so main.c and calc.h do not change:.

It has been revealed that typec compiles calc.tc to an ordinary object. The C compiler links it with the main.o of the C build, which is not even recompiled:.

A command added to command later, such as Mul(long n), stops the build at every match that does not handle it.

A build compiles calc.tc with typec, and its other files as before (In a build).

A C11 translation unit is a Type-C unit with the same meaning (design 2.2): each Type-C construct begins with tokens that C refuses, and the words Type-C adds, such as type, match and result, stay free for C's identifiers (design 2.3). So a file renamed to .tc compiles before any Type-C is written in it, and while it uses no Type-C construct, typec hands the C compiler its preprocessed text byte for byte: the object equals the one that the C compiler builds from that same preprocessed text with the same options (test/run/pipeline.t). The corpus runner checks the same on every file of real programs, among them zlib, Lua, SQLite and QBE, each renamed to .tc (Running the corpus); recording a run of the whole corpus at one revision on every host is open in TODO.md.

The fine print, for a .tc file:.

In a recent development, the code that you write in Type-C compiles to plain C (What the C looks like). Of the code that the compiler adds without the source spelling it out, the traps of matching, the cleanups of defer and slice bounds checks are built; checked mode will add the rest (principle 4). The rest of a program links as before: Type-C functions are C functions under their own names, with no mangling, and typec adds no library to the link (design 10.4). Debuggers step through the lines of the .tc file (design 13.6), but the debug information is not yet that of a direct compile: with Clang it names a temporary file as the compilation unit, and on macOS a command that links a .tc input with other inputs loses the .dSYM of -g (TODO.md).

According to recent reports, in a build, typec is the C compiler, with the backend that TYPEC_CC names (Choosing the backend). It hands main.c and every other C file to the backend untouched, so a build tool needs to learn only that a .tc file is compiled as a .c file is. The dependency options (-M, -MM, -MD, -MMD, -MF, -MT, -MQ, -MP) work as for a .c file: the rule of calc.o names calc.tc and every header and .tci interface that it includes, so make or ninja rebuilds calc.o when one of them changes, and nothing when none does.

In a GNU Makefile, the rule for a .tc file is make's built-in rule for a .c file:.

With ninja, whose deps = gcc reads the same dependency files:.

In CMake, a file of rules that CMake reads when it enables C makes .tc a suffix of C sources:.

Sources indicate that the LANGUAGE C property on calc.tc would not do: with it, CMake puts -x c before the file, and typec then hands it to the backend as C, as the C compiler would take it. The tests make_rule.t, ninja_rule.t and cmake_rule.t build with these rules on both backends, where the host has the tool.

typec stops at the first error it finds, prints it as GCC and Clang print theirs, file:line: error: message with the line of the source under it, and exits with status 80. The line has no caret: the C compiler preprocesses the source, so the error names a line and no column (design 13.6). An error under a rule of Type-C ends with the rule's name in brackets, as [match-arm-end], the way GCC ends a warning with its option; the catalogue of diagnostics (dune build docs/diagnostics.md writes it to _build/default/docs/diagnostics.md) gives each name's rule and the section of the design that states it. A message about no place in the source, as one about the command line, begins with typec: instead. An error that the C compiler finds in the C that typec writes, as with the generic types above, comes with the C compiler's message and status. test/run/readme.t checks the files and the output of every C and Type-C example on this page, on GCC and Clang.

Sources indicate that typec writes plain C11 with the GNU extensions that GCC and Clang share, and --emit-c prints it. A variant is a structure of an enumeration, its tag, and a union of one structure for each case that has fields. The enumeration ends with a hidden enumerator of the value INT_MAX, so the tag has the size of int with or without -fshort-enums. A match is a switch on the tag that copies the fields an arm binds into const locals, and traps after each arm and in the default that it adds for a tag that is none of the cases, beside the case of the hidden enumerator. A C switch on a tag needs a default too, or -Wswitch reports that enumerator. A distinct type is a typedef of the type it is made from, and an instance of a generic type is a structure named after its arguments, as list__i is list(int). C code and Type-C code call each other with no glue. C text that uses no Type-C construct is written out as it was read.

typec --emit-c shape.tc writes this, here without its line markers and laid out for reading:.

The unit ends with a few static assertions of what typec assumes of the target, which fail to compile where the C compiler's types differ from those typec read, as under a wrapper that adds -funsigned-bitfields.

Industry observers note that A result is a variant like any other, an instance named after its arguments, as result__i5error is result(int, error). A try tests the tag and returns the error at once, and a defer writes its statement at each exit of its scope, in reverse order, after the value of a return is computed: the C of early returns that each release what is held, with no table, unwinding or allocation.

typec --emit-c pair.tc writes this, here without its line markers and laid out for reading:.

A tag that is neither Ok nor Err traps, as in every match, and so does the end of the function, which no path reaches.

According to recent reports, the lowering is measured against hand-written C: Type-C programs and C twins of them, which carry the same checks (the trap of a match on a bad tag, the copies of the bound fields), are built at -O2 with both compilers and compared in code size and in the instructions they retire (Measuring against hand-written C). The cost of the checks themselves, and what is not measured yet, are open in TODO.md.

C code sees what design 10.6 lists: a variant is the structure shown above, a distinct type is the type it is made from, and a function is the same C function. The C compiler lays out both sides, so they agree: test/run/abi.t links objects that typec builds with objects of the C compiler alone, in every pairing of GCC and Clang, and passes variants with fields of each class of C object type both ways, the C side reading them through a structure written by hand as design 10.1 gives it.

Recent findings suggest that one header can serve both kinds of file. typec defines __TYPEC__ while it preprocesses a Type-C unit, so the header can give Type-C files a distinct type where C files see a plain typedef (design 2.1). Both have the same representation, so both call the same function, and only the Type-C side gets the check:.

It has been revealed that typec --emit-c-header M.tci writes M.h, the C header of a .tci interface, so that C code gets its variants without a structure written by hand (design 9.3). A Type-C unit that includes M.h reads M.tci itself. The dependency options work as for a .tc file, with the header as the target of the rule, which names M.tci and every file that it includes: -MD and -MMD write the rule to M.h.d, the header's path followed by .d, or to the file that -MF names, so a makefile rule M.h: M.tci whose command is typec --emit-c-header -MMD -MP M.tci, with -include M.h.d beside it, rebuilds M.h when an interface that M.tci includes changes. -M and -MM print the rule, or write it to the -MF file, and write no header, so they cannot be used with -o. Under -o - no path names the header, and -MD and -MMD need -MT or -MQ and -MF.

Pilot B, the plan's test of Stage 2 on real code (plan, Stage 2), rewrote the parser of tomlc99, a TOML library in C (toml.c, 2392 lines), with result, try and defer. Its header toml.h, its C programs and its tests did not change and link against the Type-C object. The pilot's repository is not published; the numbers here are from its record.

Fault injection fails each allocation of a parse in turn, one run for each. Over the library's 62 example files, 1416 runs, the original went wrong in 34: 25 leaks and 9 uses after free, from two defects in the code that grows an array or a table. The rewrite went wrong in none, built by Clang or GCC, and the address, undefined behavior and leak sanitizers reported nothing. Over the 146 files of toml-spec-tests, 18847 runs, the original leaked in 1022, 1000 of them in one deeply nested file, and crashed in 9; the rewrite did neither.

try and defer did not remove the defects by themselves. A variant of the rewrite whose three faulty functions only put a try in place of each if (!x) return kept all 34 bad runs. Adding a defer that frees each new object until it is linked into the tree removed the 25 leaks but not the 9 uses after free, which came from the order of the steps: the old buffer of an array was freed before its new element existed. Reordering the steps, so that each grown buffer is stored and counted before the next allocation, removed them. The language puts the question "who owns this object if this step fails?" at every try; the rewrite had to answer it.

What it costs, at -O2 -g, against a hand-written C version of the same rewrite with a goto cleanup where Type-C has a defer:.

According to recent reports, the record does not split the rest of the growth further and puts most of it down to the representation of result, a structure of a tag and a union returned by value where the C returns an int or a pointer; returning a result whose error has no fields as the bare value is open in TODO.md. Parse times are the best of five rounds, and repeated runs move each by 2 to 3 percent, more than any gap between the versions. Error paths were not timed.

One line each on the principles of design section 1, which states them in full:.

...turn on more warnings, or run an analyzer? Use them: Type-C code still gets the warnings of the C compiler. Warnings see only the forms they were written for, and no flag that comparison.t tries catches a read of the wrong member, swapped ids or a value made outside its module. An analyzer finds what the paths it explores reach. In Type-C these mistakes are type errors that every build checks, with no extra tool.

Industry observers note that ...use Rust, Zig or OCaml? All three have tagged unions whose matches are checked for missing cases, and generic types, and safe Rust and OCaml are memory safe, which Type-C is not (design 14). All three call C, but C code gains their checks only when it is rewritten in their language, and the build gains their toolchain and a boundary between the languages: Rust reads C's declarations through extern "C" blocks, written by hand or generated by bindgen, Zig translates C headers into Zig, and OCaml calls C through stubs written against its runtime, which brings a garbage collector. typec is a tool to add too, but in Type-C the checks start in the one file you rename. It includes the same headers as they are, is compiled by the same C compiler, and gives an object with the C ABI, which links with the rest as before (Adopting one file).

...use C++? std::variant, enum class and templates do much of this, in another language. A C file is not always a C++ file (int *p = malloc(n); is an error in C++), C++ reaches C functions through extern "C" declarations, and C++ brings exceptions and a runtime library to link. A C file stays valid Type-C, and typec writes C.

Sources indicate that ...write macros? A macro that writes struct { T *data; ... } makes a new type at each use, so the VECTOR(int) of one declaration does not pass where another VECTOR(int) is wanted, and C refuses the call. The usual fix declares each instance once by name, by hand. A generic type such as vector(int) is one type wherever it is written. A macro cannot check a switch either.

Type-C 1.0 is the core language, frozen: variants, match, if (case ...) and nested patterns, distinct types, private and interface files (.tci), generic types and functions, option and result, try and defer, and slices with checked indexing and str. typec --emit-c-header writes the C header of an interface for C clients. The design specifies the whole language, and the strategy built it in stages, each ending in a measured gate, and the three pilots build with this release (Measured on a real library).

The test suite passes with Clang and with GCC on macOS, x86-64 and arm64, and on Linux, with glibc on x86-64 and with musl on x86-64 and arm64 (Building and testing).

Designed and not yet implemented: a checked mode, whose rules are provisional, that rules out specific classes of memory errors in the functions it covers (Stage 5 of the initiative).

You need OCaml, dune and a GCC or Clang, of the releases that Building and testing names. From a checkout, with the examples above saved under their names:.

typec takes the command line of cc and hands an input that is not a .tc file to the C compiler untouched, so an existing build runs with CC=typec and its C files compile as before. With a .tc input it refuses the few options that it cannot follow, such as -E, which stops before the C it writes, or -funsigned-bitfields, which changes C's types, and the long options, spelled with --, that it does not know. The C compiler is cc unless --cc=PATH or TYPEC_CC names another (choosing it).

examples/ holds larger programs, each beside the C that it ports, such as FreeBSD's cut(1).

It has been revealed that requirements: OCaml 5.4 and dune 3; the tests also need a C compiler as cc, a Clang and a GCC of releases that typec supports (see Choosing the backend), and tools/corpus/runner.t runs /usr/bin/clang. The cram tests in test/run run the Clang that TYPEC_TEST_CLANG names and the GCC that TYPEC_TEST_GCC names; unset, they are /usr/bin/clang and the gcc-16 on the PATH, those of a macOS host with Homebrew's GCC (test/run/backends.sh). headers.t parses and reads the declarations of every C11 and POSIX header that each backend's system headers hold. target.t expects the model of x86-64, of arm64 Linux or of arm64 macOS, and types.t, declarations.t and expressions.t compile for the host's target and for a second one, -m32 on x86-64 and the other signedness of plain char elsewhere (second_target in test/run/backends.sh). A host without the C headers of i386 runs the tests that include the C headers (abi.t) with the other signedness of plain char instead of -m32, and dune test prints a line saying so. A host that has them sets TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_M32 to a non-empty value, and dune test then fails when the backends do not both compile with -m32; the check is a rule of test/run/dune, so a run of one test alone (dune test test/run/abi.t) skips it. short_enums.t and c_header.t also run the arm-none-eabi-gcc that TYPEC_TEST_ARM_GCC names, or the one on the PATH, where present, and Clang for thumbv7m-none-eabi where Clang has that target. The rule that reports -m32 also prints which of the two Arm backends ran and which were skipped, and fails when one is missing and TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_ARM is set to a non-empty value. tutorial.t runs its lldb examples where the lldb on the PATH debugs the programs of both backends; the same rule prints whether they run on this host, and fails when they do not and TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_LLDB is set to a non-empty value. The sanitized tests add AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer on each backend that links them; the rule prints whether each backend does, and fails when one does not and TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_SANITIZERS is set to a non-empty value. There are no other dependencies.

dune exec typec -- ARGS runs the compiler from the build tree.

tools/gate.sh is the command to run before a commit: it runs dune build, dune build @check and dune test, then builds the typing oracle and runs its tests, which dune test skips (see Typing oracle). It needs the opam switch tools and fails, saying where to find how to create it, when the switch is missing. Before its steps it prints that report, which dune test writes only to the log, so a skipped Arm backend reveals, and stops where a TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_* variable of test/run/backends.sh names one that is missing. It prints the end of the log when a step fails; the variables in the header of the script set the opam root, the oracle's build directory and the log.

According to recent reports, library tests are in test/unit; the parser's are tables of C text and the structural dump of its tree (test/support/tree_dump.ml) or its error. test_deep_trees runs every chain that the parser reads in a loop (test/support/chains.ml), as deep as Parser.max_depth lets it, through the stages after the parser on a stack limited to 256K words of amd64 frames (more where a frame is larger). test/golden holds cram tests that show the C or the diagnostic that the front end gives for a source, with no backend (test/golden/golden.ml); dune test test/golden runs them and dune promote takes a changed output. Every rule that typec enforces has a stable name in the one table src/syntax/rule_table/rule_table.ml, which generates the module Rule and the catalogue _build/default/docs/diagnostics.md (dune build docs/diagnostics.md); test/golden/coverage.ml fails while some rule's name appears in no golden output, so a upcoming rule needs a golden case, and test/golden/citations.ml fails while an expected output of a golden or run test states the word "design": a diagnostic says what is wrong in the terms of the user's text, and its rule name is the reference. test/run holds cram tests that run typec and the backends; types.t and declarations.t compile static assertions of what typec computes, so a backend that disagrees fails to compile them. test/misuse holds OCaml that an interface must refuse; each file names its library and the expected error text in a (* misuse: LIBRARY TEXT *) line, and passes only when ocamlc rejects it with that text.

Recent findings suggest that the backend is the program named by the last --cc=PATH option, else by the TYPEC_CC environment variable when it is set and not empty, else cc. A name without a slash is looked up in PATH. typec consumes --cc=, --print-target, --emit-c, --emit-c-header, --stats, --trap-function= and --version where an option can stand (the value of -o is never one) and forwards every other argument, --cc without = included, in its original order. The backend is run with an argument vector, never through a shell, so TYPEC_CC names one program: it cannot carry extra arguments such as ccache gcc.

According to recent reports, A backend that runs typec again, such as a cc first on PATH that is typec itself, is refused: typec sets TYPEC_OUTER_CC to the backend's name in the environment of every backend it runs, and a typec that starts with it set exits with 81 after one message naming that backend. The whole process tree of the backend inherits the mark, so a typec that a wrapper backend runs on purpose is refused too. To install typec as cc, set TYPEC_CC to the path of the real C compiler.

Recent findings suggest that the backend is GCC or Clang, Apple's included, no older than the releases that minimum_major_version in src/sema/target.ml names. typec refuses an older one with a message naming the oldest supported releases.

Without a .tc input typec replaces itself with the backend. Exit status: the backend's own; a backend ended by a signal ends typec with the same signal. typec exits with 81 when --cc= has no path, --trap-function= names no C identifier or one reserved to typec, the backend cannot be started or the backend runs typec again, after one message on stderr (with --print-target, a second notes that the backend gave no target model).

typec's own failures have statuses of their own, which src/driver/exit_status.ml defines and design 13.2 explains: 80 when it refuses the program (a diagnostic about the source), 81 for an error of its environment (the command line, the backend, a file it cannot read or write) and 82 for an internal error, a bug in typec. Every other status is the backend's.

An input whose name ends in .tc, with no -x other than -x none before it, goes through three steps:.

On Clang, steps 1 and 3 also get -Wno-unused-command-line-argument before OPTIONS, so that Clang does not warn about an option of the command line that the step does not use. GCC does not know the option, so its steps go without it. The query for the target model runs before the backend is known and gets it on both.

Industry observers note that -std=gnu17 is left out when the command line gives -std= for C11 or C17 (c11, c17, c18, gnu11, gnu17, gnu18, c1x, gnu1x, iso9899:2011, iso9899:2017, iso9899:2018); any other -std= is a usage error. Step 2 reads asm and typeof as keywords in the GNU forms and as identifiers in the ISO forms, as GCC and Clang do; -fasm and -fno-asm select the GNU and the ISO keywords whatever -std= notes. The options of step 1 are those that matter to preprocessing and to code generation, those of step 3 the latter only; src/driver/cc_option.ml is the one table that tells them apart and says which options take a separate value. The output is named as cc names it: after -o, else after the input in the current directory. When the command line links and has no input but .tc ones, step 3 is the final command: the backend compiles and links the command line with each .tc input replaced by -x cpp-output EMITTED, where EMITTED is named as the input with the suffix .c, in a directory of its own. The backend thus leaves what it leaves for a one-step build of C sources, named as there: on macOS the .dSYM bundle of -g, and the files of -gsplit-dwarf, -fstack-usage and -fcallgraph-info. When the command line links with other inputs, each .tc input becomes an object in the temporary directory and the backend links the command line with those objects in place of the .tc inputs, and the side outputs of step 3 are lost with the objects; without linking, the other inputs are compiled by one more backend command without the .tc inputs. A .c input is thus compiled exactly as without typec.

In a recent development, with -MD or -MMD the dependency file comes from step 1, named as cc names it: after -MF, else after -o with the suffix .d, else after the input; its target is the -MT or -MQ value, else the real output. With -M or -MM the command line compiles nothing: step 1 of each .tc input prints its rule in place of the preprocessed text, to the -o file or stdout, and one more backend command gets the command line without the .tc inputs, when other inputs remain, to print theirs.

--emit-c stops after step 2 and writes the C to the -o file, or to stdout; the command line then has exactly one input, a .tc file.

In a recent development, --trap-function=NAME makes every trap of the emitted C (a corrupted tag, a slice index out of range) call _Noreturn void NAME(void), which the program supplies, instead of executing __builtin_trap() alone; a freestanding program uses it to report the failure (design 10.5). NAME is a C identifier of ASCII letters, digits and underscores outside the names reserved to typec, which begin with __tc_, and the last --trap-function= wins. NAME is the name the program defines, not a macro: the emitted C is already preprocessed, so -DNAME=... does not change it. A .tc unit that holds a Type-C construct declares NAME after its own text, so a declaration of NAME in the program with another type is a backend error reported at typec's text ().

In a recent development, --stats prints on stderr, for each .tc input and for the .tci input of --emit-c-header, one line typec: stats: FILE: and the fields unit_bytes (the preprocessed unit), instance_bytes (charged to the instance budget), copy_bytes (the front end's charge to the output limit for the copies of deferred statements, which output_bytes counts again), output_bytes (charged to the output limit by lowering, the unit's own text included, and for a header then every byte of the header, its macro brackets and macro probe among them), output_limit, longest_instance_code (the most bytes of the code of one instance, its generic's name and the encodings of its arguments, that the bound on encodings holds) and longest_name (of a type declaration or a generic function, the universe text included), each as name=value: the counts of design 3.5 rule 7 that the measurements of P30 read. Then come the slice tests of the unit and of each instance that it uses, which the measurements of P28 read: slice_indexes, slice_subs and slice_conversions (those that C evaluates, which lowering writes with a test), slice_untested (those that C does not evaluate) and slice_late_calls (the tested indexes and slice_subs with a call or a statement expression in an operand after the first). Last come the most steps (selection_steps), nodes (selection_nodes) and nodes on one path (selection_depth) that building the selection tree of one match or test of the unit or of an instance took, which the measurements of P32 read, each the most over all of them. The holders of a try of the unit and of each instance come last, which the measurements of P33 to P35 read: try_holders (the holders), try_tries (their try expressions), try_first_operands (the hoisted operands that are the first operand of &&, || or a conditional operator or the left operand of a comma), try_conditioned (the hoisted operands under a condition) and try_multiple (the holders with more than one hoisted operand). A unit that typec refuses reports none.

A .tc input refuses the option that stops the backend at preprocessing (-E), the options that change the preprocessed text (-P, -C, -CC, -fuse-line-directives, -traditional-cpp, -fdirectives-only), every -d option of dumps (-dD, -dM, -dI and the like), alone or passed on by -Wp,, -Xpreprocessor or -Xclang (which so refuses Clang's -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone too), -save-temps, -###, -ansi, --, the options that name a file of further options (response files, @FILE, -specs= and --config=) and the queries that print a fact of the backend (-print-file-name= and every other -print- option, -dumpmachine), with a usage error naming the option. It refuses a long option, spelled with --, that it does not know, as GCC reads --NAME as -fNAME and accepts abbreviations, so that --preprocess, --write-user-dep or --short-enums cannot reach the backend unseen; an option that also has a form with one - passes in that form. It refuses the options known to change a type of C without changing a macro that the target model reads, which the model therefore cannot see: -funsigned-bitfields or -fno-signed-bitfields, and -fsingle-precision-constant, even when a later option undoes them. -fshort-enums passes: the target query learns the enumeration representation by its probe compiles (Printing the target model). Other routes to these types, such as a config file, a wrapper or a target whose default differs, fail in step 3: the C of a unit with a Type-C construct ends, after a line marker for with flag 3, with a static assertion of each such type that typec assumes, whose message names the option that would break it; that of the enumeration rule also states the representation that typec expects. Flag 3 keeps the user's warning options off typec's own text. An option that changes a macro the model reads, such as -funsigned-char or -fshort-wchar, reaches the target model. It refuses -fpack-struct without a value, under which GCC ignores the #pragma pack lines that typec writes around an instance of a generic and warns of each; -fpack-struct=n passes. A unit that holds such lines also ends with a probe that fails where the backend reads #pragma pack() as a pop, as Clang does under -fapple-pragma-pack. It also refuses -arch options that name more than one architecture: cc builds a universal binary from them, but step 1 preprocesses for one architecture only. Build each architecture with its own -arch and join the results with lipo -create.

It has been revealed that A freestanding build passes -ffreestanding -nostdlib as for C. The objects need from the environment what the same C needs, such as memset, and nothing more: a trap is __builtin_trap(), an instruction on x86-64 and AArch64 (design 10.4).

According to recent reports, the temporary directory is made with mode 0700 in TMPDIR, or /tmp, and removed on every way out. SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGPIPE, SIGQUIT and SIGTERM are passed on to the running backend; typec then removes the directory and ends by the same signal.

Exit status: 0 when every step succeeds; else the status of the first backend step that fails, or the signal that ended it; 80 when the reader or the front end refuses the preprocessed text; 81 for a usage error, when the backend cannot be started or gives no target model, or when a file cannot be read or written; 82 for an internal error.

typec --print-target [OPTIONS] runs the backend as BACKEND OPTIONS -dM -E -x c /dev/null and prints the target model that its predefined macros give: the backend and its major version, the sizes of the scalar types, the signedness of char, the types behind size_t and the other standard typedefs, the byte order and __STDC_VERSION__, one field: value per line, and last the enumeration representation, int-sized or short (as under -fshort-enums), which no macro states: typec learns it by two compiles of a probe, BACKEND OPTIONS -fsyntax-only -w -dumpdir DIR/ -x c -, each of which compiles under one representation alone. Whether the backend has __float128, among the optional floating types, comes from a third compile of the same form, since no macro indicates so on every target. The other arguments are the backend options that select the target or the dialect, such as -m32, -funsigned-char or -std=gnu17; inputs, -o and dependency options do not belong there.

Exit status: 0 with the model on stdout; 81 when the backend fails, cannot be started, is not supported or prints macros the model cannot be read from, when it compiles neither probe or both, or for a usage error; 82 for an internal error.

Industry observers note that typec --version runs BACKEND --version, passes on its output, then prints typec and its release on a last line, such as typec 1.0. A build tool that tells compilers apart by the output of $CC --version, such as Meson, or a script that reads its first line thus sees the backend. The rest of the command line does not reach the backend and nothing is compiled, as GCC and Clang compile nothing with their --version; an error in one of typec's own options, such as --cc= without a path, is still one. The status is the backend's, or 81 when it cannot be started, or 0 when SIGPIPE ended the backend and the reader of the output is gone, as a reader such as head -1 that stops early is no failure; a backend that fails or cannot be started is named on stderr, and typec's line is still printed. The release has one source, the version field of dune-project, which the build writes into typec; a release tag vX.Y is made after it is set.

docs/typec.1, in mdoc(7), is installed by dune install as man/man1/typec.1 under the prefix, or under the directory of --mandir. test/unit/test_manual.ml checks its lists of typec's options and exit statuses against the driver's tables, and mandoc -Tlint -Wwarning docs/typec.1 checks its markup.

The test hosts, fuzzing, the corpus runner, the typing oracle and the measurements against hand-written C are described in docs/development.md. The order of work is the implementation proposal, and open work is in TODO.md.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling newly introduced approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, halide 3.4 is out today as the latest revision to the pro camera app.
  • The new Halide revision also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash.
  • According to recent reports, lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, halide 3.4 is out today as the latest revision to the pro camera app. The update adds several upcoming features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide revision also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

According to recent reports, lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Sources indicate that today’s fresh XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

Recent findings suggest that in low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Industry observers note that halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The revision revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

According to recent reports, halide Mark III rolled out back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of fresh features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

Industry observers note that but Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a latest setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

It has been revealed that while wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.
