📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Sources indicate that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save significant on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Sources indicate that the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the firm introduced a fresh model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

It has been revealed that if you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's right now pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

According to recent reports, if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (at the moment $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

Recent findings suggest that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

It has been revealed that follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

According to recent reports, no. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

Jon McCormack spent eight years at Apple and “oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how owners capture, view, and edit their pictures and video.”.

Industry observers note that 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Mark Gurman reports that Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to replace McCormack, who reported to software chief Craig Federighi. “Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under other executives,” the report says.

In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:.

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. This year, Apple added a variable-aperture camera to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, giving consumers more control over lighting and depth of field. The tech giant also introduced a customizable Camera app interface with professional controls.

Industry observers note that bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report claims.

It has been revealed that mcCormack spoke in depth about iOS 27 features like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing in an interview with Tyler Stalman in June. He emphasized how the features “preserve the integrity of the moment.”.

If You Loved 'The Diplomat,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary).
  • It has been revealed that if you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S.
  • Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

It has been revealed that if you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

Recent findings suggest that when a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

According to recent reports, it’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating newly introduced crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more cynical diplomats, secret plans, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that if your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and releases a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that this might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a golf writer, I get to play at some pretty incredible courses.
  • But when I received an invite to Mexico to experience Gourmet and Golf at Punta Mita, I almost fell out of my chair with excitement.
  • Industry observers note that and I made the right decision in more ways than one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a golf writer, I get to play at some pretty incredible courses. The USGA brought me out to Winged Foot to check out its new app, and it was one of the most incredible golf experiences I've ever had.

But when I received an invite to Mexico to experience Gourmet and Golf at Punta Mita, I almost fell out of my chair with excitement. I've never been to Mexico, and I've never played golf outside of the United States, so going was a no-brainer.

Industry observers note that and I made the right decision in more ways than one. Yes, the golf was great, but this event completely changed my life for the better. Seriously.

I attended the 15th anniversary of Punta Mita's Gourmet and Golf, which led the resorts (St. Regis Punta Mita Resort and the Four Seasons Resort Punta Mita) to go a little crazy with the number and quality of chefs. But any year you go, the food and golf will be incredible, and I personally can't wait to see how good the event is for its 20th anniversary.

According to recent reports, if you decide to attend, you're looking at $3,599 for a 3-night package and $4,399 for the four-night (I did three, and it was enough time to play two rounds of golf and eat until I felt I might pop). This includes a beautiful place to stay, all ultra-high-end meals, participation in the Punta Mita Golf Cup over 2 days at both Jack Nicklaus Signature Golf Courses, transportation to and from the airport, and more.

It's not cheap, but the value is there — how often do you get to indulge in three days of top-of-the-line food and two days of premium Jack Nicklaus Signature Golf (with one day playing out as a two-person scramble and one as a best ball event)?

Sources indicate that this feels weird to say for me after 40 years of being overwhelmingly picky, but I was a super picky eater. Saying "was" just doesn't feel right, but going to Gourmet and Golf actually helped me break out of my picky-eating habits.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sure, it's only been a couple of weeks, and I have to keep the momentum going by continuing to try newly introduced foods, but I feel confident saying I was a picky eater, not that I am one.

It has been revealed that I figured that since Gourmet and Golf features some of the world's best chefs, it would be the perfect chance to let my guard down and try whatever was put in front of me. So I did. I tried foods that would normally make me recoil in fear. I ate caviar, tacos and things I can't even pronounce; things I don't even remember. I tried shrimp, lobster and other foods I've had in the past and didn't like. I confirmed I still don't like them, but I tried them without hesitation.

Sources indicate that it was like a food blur, and just about everything I tried was great. I counted for the first couple of days of the trip, but eventually the whirlwind of latest foods became too much. I'd guess I tried at least 40 new foods.

If you're a picky eater like me, Gourmet and Golf could change your approach to food if you let it. And if you're not a picky eater (like my girlfriend Andria, who accompanied me on the trip), then you're in for a treat, because the food is some of the best you can get. There's a reason these are Michelin-starred chefs — they know what they're doing.

Okay, so the food was good. It changed my life and helped me overcome my fear of trying upcoming foods. Good for me, right? But how were the Nicklaus-designed Bahia and Pacifico golf courses?

I keep track of my golf course ratings on a cool app called Eden. In it, Winged Foot West is my number one course — it gets 10 on my rating scale. Now, though, it has another course nipping at its heels, with the Pacifico course at Punta Mita getting a 9.9. And it's close — while ranking the courses, I actually considered putting Punta Mita above Winged Foot West based primarily on the blend of incredible vistas and the overall quality of the golf.

In the end, the history and legacy offered by Winged Foot gave it a slight edge, but it's close. And the Bahia course isn't far behind, coming in as the 7th best course I've ever played (beaten by Winged Foot West, Tamarack Country Club, Pacifico, Country Club of Waterbury, Scottsdale National and PGA National). Between the two courses, Punta Mita is clearly a destination with golfers in mind.

Sources indicate that to give you an idea of some of the other courses with the Nicklaus pedigree, we're talking about The Saint Andrews Golf Club, Great Bear Golf Club, Bayside, Champion Course at PGA National, Harbour Town Golf Links, Nicklaus Course at PGA West and the list goes on and on. Punta Mita's golf courses come with some serious pedigree, and they live up to the challenge for which Nicklaus is known.

Which would explain why I shot a 115 during the best ball portion of the tournament.

These are hard golf courses designed to test every aspect of your golf game with massive, intelligently placed bunkers, narrow fairways, undulating greens, false fronts and all the other tricks that rack up strokes.

According to recent reports, but nothing about the design feels haphazard or just there to make things difficult. It's all built to reward smart course management and good shots — something I was apparently incapable of during this particular trip (to give you some perspective, I typically shoot in the mid-to-upper 90s, so I shot almost 20 strokes more than normal).

Industry observers note that you know what? I don't care. My partner didn't care. It's hard to care what you shoot when you're surrounded by such beautiful scenery, like you are on both the Bahia and Pacifico courses at Punta Mita. And when the round was over, I knew I had some of the best culinary delights I've ever experienced waiting for me (and strategically placed around the two courses).

In a recent development, it doesn't matter what you shoot; you will have a good time at Gourmet and Golf. Just ask my partner — she didn't even play golf and can't stop talking about going back for another year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Linux のデスクトップを、Windows XP のシェルで。.

個人の実験的なプロジェクトです。 日常の作業環境として使えるほど完成してはいません。 動作を確かめているのは、新しくインストールした Debian 13 に導入スクリプトで入れた場合だけです。 すでに使っている環境（ほかのデスクトップ環境やディスプレイマネージャが入っているものなど）への導入は試していません。 試すときは、仮想マシンや試験用のマシンをおすすめします。.

Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを当てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェルとして動かすプロジェクトです。 タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。.

Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。.

XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル（Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも 試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、導入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（docs/reactos.md）。.

Windows 7 の ISO があれば、Windows 7 のシェル（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（docs/windows7.md）。.

XP の ISO が無いときは、ReactOS のシェルで試せます（ISO は要りません）。.

ログイン画面でセッション「ReactOS Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。.

Windows 7 のシェル（実験的）は、Windows 7 SP1 x64 の ISO から作ります。.

ログイン画面でセッション「Windows 7 Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。.

詳しい手順とオプションは 🔗 導入手順（INSTALL.md） にあります。Wine をソースからビルドするので、4 コアで 1 時間半ほどかかります。 テーマ（XP のクラシックなど）と文字の大きさは、後から変えられます（見た目と文字の大きさを変える）。.

LGPL-2.1-or-later（Wine と同じ）です。対象はこのリポジトリのコードとパッチだけです。 ただし wayland/patches/labwc/ は labwc と同じ GPL-2.0-only、wayland/patches/wlroots/ は wlroots と同じ MIT です。 Windows XP と Windows 7 のファイルと、スクリーンショットに写っている XP と Windows 7 の画面の著作権は Microsoft にあります。 ReactOS のシェルで使う ReactOS のファイルは、ReactOS のライセンス（GPL-2.0-or-later、DLL の多くは LGPL-2.1-or-later）に従います。.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

It has been revealed that many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

Industry observers note that to use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see new “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

Tech Report: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • Industry observers note that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

Industry observers note that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

In a recent development, during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

In a recent development, an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

In a recent development, he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs highlights the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

Sources indicate that on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

According to recent reports, the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most vital processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Industry observers note that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she claims, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, rolled out in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

Sources indicate that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

It has been revealed that the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

According to recent reports, capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

In a recent development, the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

Sources indicate that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Industry observers note that since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller claims wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller indicates with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

In a recent development, but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” states Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

According to recent reports, as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

Recent findings suggest that the countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

In a recent development, among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller states with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

It has been revealed that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

In a recent development, with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

It has been revealed that the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller claims. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

I played GTA 6 without a TV all weekend — and kept Vice City to myself with AR glasses

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after 13 long years, the wait is finally over, and like many of you, I couldn’t wait to load up GTA 6 for the first time this weekend.
  • Sources indicate that with a game this massive and this anticipated, the last thing you want is to be interrupted — or worse, unable to play because someone else in your household claimed the TV first.
  • For those of us with a significant other or kids at home, though, carving out the necessary time to finally play GTA 6 hasn’t been that easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after 13 long years, the wait is finally over, and like many of you, I couldn’t wait to load up GTA 6 for the first time this weekend. However, instead of playing on the largest screen in my house, I decided that a pair of AR glasses might be the best way to experience this latest and improved Vice City. Let me explain.

Sources indicate that with a game this massive and this anticipated, the last thing you want is to be interrupted — or worse, unable to play because someone else in your household claimed the TV first. Now, if you’re an adult who lives by yourself and got to play GTA 6 sprawled out on your couch with one of the best OLED TVs, more power to you.

For those of us with a significant other or kids at home, though, carving out the necessary time to finally play GTA 6 hasn’t been that easy. Fortunately for me, I knew there was another way instead of trying to sneak in a late-night play session in front of the TV.

You see, over the summer on a trip to Taiwan for Computex, I spent almost my entire 17-hour flight playing Red Dead Redemption on the Switch 2 in AR glasses. That got me thinking: what if I tried playing GTA 6 the same way? Well, that’s exactly what I did, and I don’t think I’d be nearly as far in the game right now if I hadn’t.

Here’s why you, too, might want to consider donning a pair of AR glasses—or more accurately, display glasses — to take in the sights, sounds, and excitement that Vice City has to offer in GTA 6.

In a recent development, this bundle has everything you need to start playing your game consoles in AR. You get a pair of Viture Pro 2 XR glasses and the Viture Pro Mobile Dock. This way you can plug your Switch 2 in directly over USB-C or consoles like the PS5 or Xbox Series X in over HDMI and the included dock brings massive-screen console gaming right to your glasses. Alternatively, if you only initiative on playing your Switch 2 this way, you can pick up the Viture Pro 2 Mini Dock Pack for $375 (down from 428) right now.

With a gaming PC or even a handheld like the Steam Deck, playing with AR glasses is as simple as plugging them in. On a console, though, it’s not that easy. Fortunately, Viture makes a few accessories to help.

It has been revealed that for instance, there’s the Viture Pro Mobile Dock and the newly introduced Viture Mobile Dock Mini. While I played RDR using the latter, when I tried playing my Switch 2 in AR glasses back at launch, I used the former. Don’t get me wrong, the new mini dock is super compact and easier to bring with you, but for playing on any console besides the Nintendo Switch, it’s missing one very important port: HDMI.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Now with the Pro Mobile Dock, in addition to USB-C out ports for two pairs of glasses — and a USB-C input for devices like the Switch 2 — you also get a full-sized HDMI port. Admittedly, I didn’t have a use for it before as I’ve mainly played games in AR glasses while traveling or on vacation, but with my PS5 Pro fired up with GTA 6 installed and ready to go, it was time to put it to the test.

I ran a long HDMI cable from the back of my console, plugged it into the dock along with a pair of the Viture Pro 2 AR glasses, powered it on, and I was good to go. GTA 6 appeared almost instantly on the Micro-OLED displays in the glasses, and since they have built-in speakers, that was all I needed.

It has been revealed that although I love their more affordable $299 price, Viture did have to cut one of my favorite features from its other glasses. Unlike the tech giant’s other models — and this is true with the Xreal XBX A01 glasses, too — there isn’t any built-in electrochromic dimming. Instead, you get a lens shade in the box.

Now, if you’ve never worn a pair of AR glasses before, electrochromic dimming lets you go from a clear display where you can see the world around you (in addition to the content from your game console, phone, or tablet) to a dimmed one without ambient light seeping through, all with the push of a button.

Sources indicate that the Viture Pro 2 glasses do have one feature going for them that made my GTA 6 play sessions a whole lot more comfortable, though. They’re extremely lightweight at just 63 grams.

Sources indicate that playing GTA 6 with AR glasses felt just like making my way through the Wild West as John Marston in RDR. I was able to take in all of Leonida without bothering anyone else in my house, and since the game runs at 30 fps, I didn’t lose anything when it came to visual quality. Now, if I were playing on PC, that would be a different story, since the Pro 2s come equipped with a 120Hz refresh rate — making them just as good for fast-paced games as they are for slower ones.

In a recent development, if you want to try something similar, you’ll get the best experience using the Pro Mobile Dock — or better yet, Viture’s new HDMI to USB-C adapter cable. Mine is still in the mail, though, so I made do with the Pro Mobile Dock, and for now, everything worked exceptionally well. However, that isn’t the only way to play GTA 6 in AR glasses.

Besides using Viture’s AR glasses with one of its docks, I’ve also spent a fair amount of time playing on a smartphone, too. If you have a newer iPhone, Samsung phone, or any smartphone with DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, you just plug your glasses in and you’re good to go. With that kind of setup, you can load up a remote play app like PXPlay (for PlayStation) or XBXPlay (for Xbox) and use a wireless controller.

That does leave your phone just lying there, which is why Viture teamed up with 8BitDo a while back to create a variant of the 8BitDo Ultimate Mobile Gaming Controller with a full-featured USB-C port. On most mobile game controllers, the USB-C ports are just used for passthrough charging. With this one, though, you can plug in a pair of AR glasses and actually get video out.

Sources indicate that just like I did during my second long-haul flight to Taiwan a few years back, I popped my Samsung Galaxy S24 FE into the controller and plugged in my AR glasses. After getting PXPlay set up on that phone, I was able to use remote play on my PS5 Pro to play GTA 6 in bed.

According to recent reports, as I was fixing up Jason’s house, though, I noticed that it was slightly difficult to see and read the button prompts on the edges of the screen. Since this was my first time playing GTA 6, I had no idea which button to press when using a nail gun to hang drywall or to fix the shingles on my roof. So I put the Pro 2s down and switched to the Viture Luma Pro glasses instead.

With the simple mission of giving you the best bang for your buck in AR glasses, Viture knocked it out the park with Luma Pro. These have the best color science of any glasses on this list, and there’s versatility in the Spacewalker software to turn any space into a giant 152-inch panoramic workspace with 3DoF tracking that keeps it anchored.

With their higher-resolution lenses (from 1080p per eye to 1200p), wider field of view (from 46 to 52 degrees), and redesigned optical stack, what was blurry on the Pro 2s became instantly clear on the Luma Pros. Now, if you’re on a tight budget and already know the controls, you can still definitely play GTA 6 with the Pro 2s. However, since I was newly introduced to the controls and had both pairs of glasses handy, making the switch was easy and absolutely worthwhile.

One feature that you’ll find on both pairs of glasses — and pretty much the rest of the AR glasses in Viture’s lineup — are myopia dials. With these, you can turn the dials to go from a blurry to a clear picture if, like me, you wear glasses or contacts. Most of the time I wear contacts, and I make it a point to have them in when wearing AR glasses. However, since I wanted to play in bed, I decided this was finally the time to try them out.

Now, I had to fully light the room in the pictures above, but on Friday and Saturday — and hopefully on Sunday evening once I’m done writing this — I cozied up in bed with that special 8BitDo controller and my AR glasses and played more GTA 6 than I’d like to admit. And frankly, it was awesome.

At first, I was a bit worried about the remote play experience with such a complex game, but with one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems equipped with Wi-Fi 7 and a fast internet connection, it worked really well.

Now, I did have my PS5 Pro plugged into my router with an Ethernet cable during those play sessions. However, when I took the pics above, I had it unplugged, and that tanked the game’s performance. So if you want to play GTA 6 remotely — with or without AR glasses — I strongly recommend connecting your console over Ethernet for a smoother and more stable remote play experience.

Industry observers note that as I’m also currently testing out the Viture Pro Neckband, I decided to put it on and go play outside for a bit of fun. While the device around my neck might look like a wearable fan, it’s actually a wearable Android tablet, if you can believe it.

Now, what I like about this setup compared to using the Pro Mobile Dock or a smartphone is that my hands weren’t weighed down and I wasn’t tethered to my console. Likewise, if you’re using a third-party app like PXPlay, you can use whatever controller you want and aren’t limited to just using a wired DualSense (like you are on PC).

Now, I must say that playing GTA 6 wasn’t nearly as good on the Pro Neckband as it was on a smartphone. Still, with my Eero Outdoor 7 mesh node on the fence behind me and seated in The Foldable Gaming Chair, it was quite comfy and still very playable. If only the weather had been Vice City sunny instead of overcast.

With a pair of AR glasses and the right dock — or even a capable smartphone — the possibilities are really endless. You’re not just limited to sitting in front of your TV or, if you have kids like I do, playing at your desk. On that second point, I haven’t seen anything too spicy — except for Mandy in a bikini — just yet, but given this is Grand Theft Auto after all, I know it’s coming. I wouldn’t want my son or my wife walking in on something inappropriate on my TV, and by playing with AR glasses on, I don’t have to worry about it.

Now, I know AR glasses, or display glasses, aren’t a must-have gadget like a smartphone, but they make for a very useful accessory. While they’re amazing on planes — and trust me, I’ve put in quite a lot of hours gaming or even watching movies with them aboard an aircraft — they’re just as useful and convenient at home.

As for me, it’s time to get back to Vice City and enjoy the quiet, slow-paced life of Chapter 1 before I eventually have to go pick up Lucia from prison.

Latest Update: Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, noted last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

Sources indicate that in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

Industry observers note that the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

What does it mean to understand what we built?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, a couple of people sent me the No AI Slop Manifesto.
  • Through this work, we have come to value: â¦ Understanding over speed.
  • I fully agree with that as a pithy statement, but I think we are working with different definitions of the word understanding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let's try come to an understanding.

Today, a couple of people sent me the No AI Slop Manifesto. I found it interesting, in part, because it touches on something that seems super crucial right now: understanding.

Through this work, we have come to value: â¦ Understanding over speed.

I fully agree with that as a pithy statement, but I think we are working with different definitions of the word understanding. For example:.

We do our own thinking when working with a model. We explore resources, code, and prior art to truly understand the problem before the work starts.

Thatâs an example of a symptom of something that I think makes this document substantially less useful and forward-looking than it could have been. Specifically, it privileges code. Thatâs natural for programmers, of course, because program text has been somewhat privileged in our fieldâs thinking for something like 60 years.

I believe that the goal of understanding code is, longer-term, holding us back from understanding what matters. Iâm excited about the possibilities of what we can understand better when we are freed from understanding code, and can focus on other things.

Sources indicate that what are those other things? The properties of the as-built system. Precise properties like âa SELECT never highlights results from uncommitted transactionsâ. And fuzzy properties like âmakes the userâs life easierâ. Those are already non-local properties that come from the code as a whole, not from any individual line. In fact, trying to understand how they are synthesized out of individual lines is a mammoth task! One that weâve spent six decades coming up with abstractions to handle.

Then there are the really emergent properties. The dynamic behaviors that only come from the system all working together. Like metastable failures. As with the Lorenz Attractor or Julia Set itâs generally intractable to extract an understanding of the behavior of these systems from the code. We need different, better, more powerful tools.

In a recent development, privileging code is, I believe, getting in the way of us really understanding what those tools should look like. The ones that help us really help understand the behavior of a system overall. Software engineering hasnât developed its Bode plots or Nyquist stability criterion yet. Or many equivalents to the kinds of tools that other fields of engineering have developed to understand complex systems as built.

Weâre still looking at each screw, each grain of aggregate, and each PCB trace, and trying to understand the whole by thinking super hard about it. Itâs time to look up. And AI gives us an incredible tool to do just that.

In a recent development, I like the manifesto. I just they didnât entirely think through what it means to be for understanding rather than against not understanding.

If you want a gaming chair that tries to do literally everything, allow me to introduce you to the DXRacer Martian Pro. It’ll massage you, heat your butt, and even cool your you-know-whats thanks to a built-in fan (which I’ve affectionately labelled “the junk wafter”).

Recent findings suggest that the Martian Pro packs lots of features, plenty of adjustment and a heavy, sturdy design. It’s also fairly comfortable as far as gaming chairs go.

It has been revealed that the best thing about the Martian Pro is its wide array of cool features. Unlike the base DXRacer Martian, the Pro has a built-in back massager, like those chairs at airports. There are loads of different modes, and the massaging is genuinely pretty good. I found myself oof-ing on quite a few occasions as the massage balls dug into tight spots on my back. This is a little annoying, but not a huge deal — I’d rather it turned itself off than keep running — and you’ll promptly get used to where your favorite massage setting is in the cycle order. I like massage setting two, which made things fairly easy.

According to recent reports, the base of the chair has a heating element, so you can warm up your butt during colder seasons. But there’s also a cooling fan for when your junk gets a little hot. As I mentioned up top, I’ve christened it “the junk wafter”. It really works, providing a strong cooling breeze. Now, given not everyone is as hygienic as I am (and I’m sure you are, dear reader), I can think of obvious downsides related to blowing air up and over the ol’ undercarriage. But hey, as long as you’re on your own at your gaming desk, who am I to judge you for cooling down your best bits?

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that you can’t heat, cool or massage without electricity, so it figures that DXRacer gave the Martian Pro electronic adjustment. The chair back is adjusted using a toggle on the left base, while the two-part lumbar pad is adjusted on the right.

Un-electronically, there’s a seat height paddle, and four-axis armrests that offer an impressive amount of adjustment (and can have their tops replaced when worn out). This lets you fine tune the chair’s shape and support.

The DXRacer Martian Pro is built pretty well. I’m not so keen on all the red accents, as I think they look a little childish and more than a little tacky, so initially I had my doubts about whether the chair would feel sturdy. But it does, for the most part.

According to recent reports, as soon as you try and get this behemoth out the box, you’ll notice it’s extremely large and very heavy, which is reassuring. The leather feels premium, there’s nice spongy padding on the armrests, and all the buttons and electronics work as they should. It never feels like it’s going to break on you.

According to recent reports, my only gripe is that the plastic side trims that cover the pivot mechanism look cheap and feel all scratchy, as a result of cheap plastic. On a nearly-$900 chair, I’d expect better.

Now, there’s a monumental caveat here: I’ll cover it in more detail later on, but in short, gaming chairs are all about show — they almost all use an inherently uncomfortable flat-backed design.

Sources indicate that that said, as gaming chairs go, this one is alright. That’s primarily thanks to the adjustable lumbar pad, which provides support for your back. It’s nowhere near as big, pronounced and supportive as the large (necessarily so) lumbar supports on the best office chairs, but better than nothing — i.e. better than the Razer Soma Chroma I tested recently. There’s also lots of padding on the arm rests and an included neck cushion (although I found this a little too large).

If you want a gaming chair that’s as comfortable as they come, check out the Razer Iskur V2 NewGen, which has a much larger lumbar pad and a decidedly ergonomic design.

Sources indicate that alas, if you want proper support and comfort, this chair isn’t for you. It needs to be charged regularly and is quite complicated to build. And there’s no way I’d recommend paying $900.

As I mentioned above, gaming chairs are almost all inherently uncomfortable. Flat backs and necks, padded rather than mesh bases, small lumbar cushions, etc. This makes their very existence weird and kinda meta: they only exist because streamers and YouTubers use them (as they look "gamer-y), which makes the general public want them too. Certain brands therefore supply the aforementioned streamers and influencers with them, which keeps the public buying them. Ah, the circle of modern life.

What I’m trying to say here is, if you want a comfortable time, do not get a gaming chair. There’s absolutely no reason why you can’t game in a luxurious office chair, and if you ask me, that’s what you should do. For the same or less money, you can get a much more comfortable and supportive chair. It's just that you won't look like a streamer.

The Martian Pro has lumbar support, yes, but even at its greatest extent it’s just a small mound. The Boulies EP460, Boulies EP500, Autonomous ErgoChair Pro and Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 all have huge mesh lumbar pads, which is what you actually need to properly support your back.

I found the Martian Pro’s neck cushion ridiculously oversized, and extremely firm, meaning no give. The result was that my head and neck were pushed forward — as if I were doing Jim Carrey’s trademark bird-like head thrust.

Recent findings suggest that worst of all is the seat pad. I have a type of immuno-arthritis that affects my legs and lower back, so it’s important my seat pads are comfortable. Let me tell you now: there is nothing quite like mesh for butt and coccyx comfort (and natural cooling as a secondary benefit). The Martian Pro uses a basic cushion, which is fairly thick, but still puts too much compression on my lower back. I had to use a coccyx cushion to stay comfortable.

Industry observers note that as I already mentioned, all those electronics above need power, which means the Martian Pro needs a cable. Now, to its credit, there’s a battery inside (and a fairly massive 5,000mAh one at that). After a full charge, the chair lasted me a few hours of massaging while gaming.

In a recent development, you need to charge it regularly, though, which I found annoying. What’s worse is that when you’ve run out of charge, you can’t adjust the recline or lumbar support as both are done electronically.

According to recent reports, it’s just too complicated for me. Again, I’d prefer the natural cooling and better analog lumbar support of a decent mesh office chair.

Thanks to all those electronics, the Martian Pro is somewhat tricky to build. While each step is fairly easy, there are just lots of them and the chair is extremely heavy — I’d recommend having two people and a lot of space before building it. You’ve also got to make sure everything is wired in properly, which can be a little confusing. I didn’t quite hide one wire properly so had to backtrack and redo my steps at one point.

In a recent development, the Martian Pro took me 42 minutes to build alone, and I was drenched in sweat afterwards. I’ve built a lot of chairs in my time as reviews editor here at Tom’s Guide, so I’m an experienced builder — I once put together the Boulies OP180 in just 10 minutes! 42 minutes is a long time for me.

Recent findings suggest that there’s absolutely no way on Earth this chair should cost $899 / £649. Sure, it has some nifty features and is built well, but it looks pretty cheap and tacky with the red accents — it’s like a five-year-old’s fever dream. To be fair, you can buy it in a plain black model, which I’d recommend. But as I mentioned above, some of the plastics used are scratchy and cheap, too.

If you want to look like your favorite streamer, and be just as uncomfortable, you can pick up the SecretLab Titan Evo for $569, which looks much more premium. Even the Razer Iskur V2 NewGen — the gold standard of gaming chairs from a comfort perspective — costs only $649 from new, which pretty well puts things into perspective: the Martian Pro is overpriced.

The DXRacer Martian Pro is unfortunately a mixed bag. It packs lots of features and is fairly comfortable for a gaming chair. It offers lots of adjustment and a sturdy build. But I can’t give this chair one of our higher scores and my outright recommendation. It’s not truly comfortable in the same way as an office chair. It’s complicated to build and needs a cable to function, and for $900 I’d expect near perfection, not to mention a premium-looking design. Maybe this one’s better suited for Mars.

The Oura Ring 5 is the world’s smallest smart ring and looks more like a piece of stylish jewelry than a fitness tracker. Though it’s rarely discounted, it’s presently seeing a record-low price of $299 (originally $399) in this early Black Friday deal.

In addition to being 40% smaller than its predecessor, the Oura Ring 5 also lasts up to nine days longer than the Oura Ring 4, and has upgraded sensors for better accuracy.
